 57th GST Council: Outdoor Catering ITC under GST - Section 17(5)(b)(i) Changes, Eligibility & Practical Examples
 CA Varun Gupta 
 CA Varun Gupta 
 Author 
 Follow 
 View profile 
 Last updated: 23 October 2026 
 Save 
 Share 
 Join Us 
 Follow Us 
 Add as Source 
 1. Introduction
 The 57th GST Council Meeting held on 8 October 2026 has proposed an important relaxation in the blocked-credit provisions under Section 17(5)(b)(i) of the CGST Act by recommending removal of the specific restriction relating to outdoor catering services. If enacted in the proposed form, the amendment could materially change the ITC position for businesses incurring genuine catering expenditure for dealer conferences, sales meetings, product launches, training programmes and other business events. However, the proposed relaxation should not be treated as a blanket entitlement to ITC on all food, meals or canteen expenditure, since classification of the service, the separate restriction on food and beverages, Section 16 conditions, exempt or personal use, supplier-side rate restrictions and place-of-supply rules may still affect eligibility. The existing law therefore needs to be compared carefully with the proposed amendment before determining the actual benefit available in each case.
 In this article, I have discussed the practical applicability of the proposed relaxation for outdoor catering ITC, the existing and proposed eligibility conditions, practical calculations, employee and business catering scenarios, documentation requirements and key precautions relating to Section 17(5)(b)(i) of the CGST Act. In case you have any doubt after reading this article, or if you feel that any practical aspect requires further discussion, you may contact me at the contact details mentioned at the end of this article.
 Important: The Council recommendation is not itself an operative amendment. The existing law continues to apply until the final provisions are brought into force. The announcement does not establish a retrospective right to claim previously blocked ITC.
 2. Existing Legal Provisions and Three Exceptions
 Section 17(5)(b)(i) restricts ITC on specified goods and services, including food and beverages and outdoor catering, notwithstanding the general business-use rule in Section 16.
 The present provision nevertheless contains exceptions:
 Same-category outward taxable supply: An inward outdoor catering service is used to make an outward taxable supply of the same category.
 Taxable composite or mixed supply: The catering service is used as an element of an outward taxable composite or mixed supply.
 Legal obligation towards employees: The employer is obligated under applicable law to provide the relevant goods or services to employees.
 CBIC Circular No. 172/04/2022-GST dated 6 July 2022 clarifies that the legal-obligation exception applies throughout Section 17(5)(b), including outdoor catering.
 Applicable service-rate conditions can independently limit ITC for catering suppliers.
 3. Case-wise Treatment of Business Meetings and Corporate Events
 The table distinguishes expenditure presently blocked under Section 17(5)(b)(i) from expenditure that may become eligible if the proposed change is enacted.
 Case 
 Practical example 
 Existing ITC position 
 After proposed change 
 1. Dealers' conference
 Manufacturer engages an outside caterer to serve 200 dealers at an annual sales conference.
 Generally blocked: business use alone does not override Section 17(5).
 Potentially eligible, subject to final wording and Section 16.
 2. Sales/marketing meeting
 Trading company provides catered food at distributor sales-target meetings.
 Generally blocked absent an existing exception.
 Potentially eligible.
 3. Product launch
 Car manufacturer caters to customers, journalists and dealers at a genuine product launch.
 Generally blocked.
 Potentially eligible if properly business-related.
 4. Employee training
 IT company hires an outdoor caterer for a two-day training workshop.
 Generally blocked absent an exception.
 Potentially eligible; employee-use issues require review.
 5. Board meeting
 Company arranges outside catering for directors during an official board meeting.
 Generally blocked.
 Potentially eligible, subject to classification and business use.
 6. Annual general meeting
 Company hires an external caterer for refreshments at its AGM.
 Generally blocked absent an exception.
 Potentially eligible, subject to business nexus.
 7. Customer technical seminar
 Engineering company caters a seminar showcasing industrial equipment.
 Generally blocked.
 Potentially eligible.
 8. Personal celebration
 Company pays for director's private marriage or birthday catering.
 Blocked as personal/non-business expenditure.
 Still not eligible: other provisions remain applicable.
 Worked Example: Dealers' Conference
 ABC Manufacturing Ltd. arranges an annual dealers' meeting to introduce new products and hires an outdoor caterer. Assume the invoice is correctly subject to 5% GST.
 Particulars 
 Amount 
 Outdoor catering charges
 Rs. 3,00,000
 GST at 5%
 Rs. 15,000
 Total catering bill
 Rs. 3,15,000
 ITC presently blocked — assuming no exception
 Rs. 15,000
 Potential ITC after effective amendment
 Rs. 15,000
 The conference may be entirely business-related, but ITC is ordinarily blocked today because the manufacturer consumes catering services at its own event.
 If the amendment is enacted in the announced form, that specific barrier may fall away.
 Maintain invitations, event agenda, attendance records, catering agreement and tax invoice.
 4. Employee Canteens and Catering Facilities
 Employee canteens require additional analysis because ITC may already be available where providing the facility is obligatory under applicable labour law.
 An additional classification issue also becomes important under the proposed amendment: not every continuing canteen or employee-meal contract necessarily constitutes “outdoor catering”. Where a service is properly classified as food and beverages or another contract food service rather than outdoor catering, deletion of the outdoor-catering restriction alone may not automatically make the credit eligible. 
 Case 
 Practical example 
 Existing ITC position 
 After proposed change 
 9. Mandatory factory canteen
 Factory required by law to maintain a canteen contracts with outside caterer.
 May already qualify under statutory-obligation exception.
 Existing entitlement may continue.
 10. Voluntary office canteen
 Company with 50 staff voluntarily provides catered lunches with no legal obligation.
 Generally blocked.
 Eligibility will depend upon whether the inward supply falls within the outdoor-catering relaxation in the final amendment or continues to be covered by the separate restriction relating to food and beverages/other contract food services.
 11. Subsidised canteen
 Employer bears 60% of canteen charges and recovers 40% from employees.
 Certain AAR/AAAR rulings limit ITC to employer-borne portion.
 Requires assessment of the final provision, service classification and treatment of employee recoveries.
 12. Contract workers
 Factory canteen serves permanent and outsourced workers.
 Requires review of labour-law obligation, employment and case law.
 May benefit depending upon statutory obligation and classification; not automatically eligible merely because the outdoor-catering restriction is proposed to be removed.
 13. Meals for visitors
 Factory canteen also serves customers and other visitors.
 Mandatory-employee exception does not automatically cover visitors.
 Business portion may benefit, subject to facts and classification.
 14. Restaurant bills
 Employees dine at a restaurant and company pays for meals.
 Generally blocked, unless current exception applies.
 Not automatically covered: food/beverages separately listed.
 15. Office pantry
 Company buys tea, coffee and snacks for daily pantry consumption.
 Generally restricted as food and beverages, subject to exceptions.
 No express general relaxation for food/beverages.
 A. Mandatory Factory Canteen
 Section 24 of the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 provides for welfare facilities, including canteens for prescribed covered establishments.
 The legal framework refers to establishments ordinarily employing 100 or more workers, including contract labour, subject to applicable Central or State rules and coverage.
 The threshold should not be applied mechanically without checking the governing rules for the establishment.
 A factory legally required to maintain a canteen may claim otherwise eligible GST on outdoor catering services supplied to discharge that obligation, subject to Section 16 and any other relevant conditions.
 Illustration: Qualifying Mandatory Factory Canteen
 Particulars 
 Amount 
 Monthly catering charges
 Rs. 2,00,000
 GST at 5%
 Rs. 10,000
 Total invoice
 Rs. 2,10,000
 Potential eligible ITC under existing exception
 Rs. 10,000
 B. Voluntary Canteen and Employee Welfare
 A company that provides free or subsidised lunches solely by management choice, without an established obligation under law, generally fails the existing statutory-obligation exception.
 The proposed amendment may benefit such expenditure where the inward supply is covered by the final outdoor-catering relaxation.
 However, if the arrangement continues to fall within the separately restricted category of food and beverages or another form of contract food service, eligibility cannot be assumed merely because “outdoor catering” is proposed to be removed from the blocked-credit provision.
 The treatment of any personal-consumption or employee-benefit element will also depend upon the final enacted wording.
 C. Employee Contribution and Partial Recovery
 Suppose a statutory factory canteen receives a contractor invoice of Rs. 1,00,000 plus Rs. 5,000 GST. The employer bears 60% of the cost, recovering 40% from employees. Certain advance/appellate advance rulings, including Tata Motors Ltd. (Gujarat AAAR, 22 December 2022), have permitted ITC on the part borne by the employer.
 Computation Under That Ruling-based Approach
 Particulars 
 Amount 
 GST in catering invoice
 Rs. 5,000
 Employer share: 60%
 Rs. 3,000
 Employee-recovered share: 40%
 Rs. 2,000
 Illustrative ITC on employer-borne portion
 Rs. 3,000
 Caution: The employer-borne ratio is not a universal statutory formula applicable to every arrangement.  
 Whether recoveries amount to consideration for an outward taxable supply, and how much ITC is allowed, depend on contractual facts, applicable law and precedents.
 D. Contract Labour
 Previous advance rulings have in some cases denied credit relating to contract workers while allowing direct-employee canteen credit.
 However, the current labour-law framework expressly includes contract labour for determining certain canteen-obligation thresholds.
 The current statutory obligation, contract terms, service classification and binding precedent must all be examined; older AAR rulings cannot be indiscriminately extended to every taxpayer.
 5. Catering Purchased for Further Outward Supply
 Case 
 Practical example 
 Treatment under existing provisions 
 16. Subcontracted catering
 ABC Caterers hires XYZ Caterers for part of ABC's taxable catering contract.
 Same-category exception may apply; check output tax rate.
 17. Composite conference service
 Event organiser purchases catering for genuine outward taxable conference package.
 Composite/mixed supply exception may apply.
 18. Supplier under 5% no-ITC rate
 Qualifying caterer sells services taxed at 5% without ITC.
 Supplier cannot override rate-based no-ITC restriction.
 19. Supplier under 18% with ITC rate
 Qualifying specified-premises caterer supplies at 18% with credit.
 Supplier credit may be available under applicable rules.
 20. Mere expense recovery
 Organiser recovers catering cost but has no qualifying onward taxable composite/mixed supply.
 Recovery alone does not establish credit exception.
 5% versus 18% - Supplier and Recipient Are Different Taxpayers
 A supplier charging 5% without ITC may not claim credit on purchases used in that supply.
 The recipient's credit on the GST charged by the supplier is determined independently under Section 17(5), Section 16 and other applicable provisions.
 Thus, a factory with a legally mandatory canteen may still have eligible ITC on a 5% catering invoice.
 Separate Same-category / Reseller Proposal
 The Council has separately proposed limited ITC for resellers of restaurant/outdoor catering services where the same category of input service is used for supplying the same category of output service.
 This is a distinct rate-related proposal and should not be understood as allowing all input tax credit to restaurant or catering suppliers.
 For example, where a caterer purchases catering service from another caterer for onward supply of catering service, the proposed limited same-category credit may be relevant. It does not by itself restore unrestricted ITC on unrelated inputs such as equipment, rent, advertising, consultancy or other expenses.
 This proposal is separate from the proposed removal of the outdoor-catering-specific restriction applicable to recipients generally.
 6. Cases Where ITC May Remain Restricted
 Removing the outdoor-catering-specific block will not override other credit restrictions, including business use, personal consumption, exempt supplies, document conditions, timing and place-of-supply rules.
 Case 
 Practical example 
 Reason / controlling condition 
 21. Private director function
 Company funds private wedding/birthday catering.
 Personal/non-business use - Sections 17(5)(g), 16(1).
 22. Unrelated private event
 Company pays catering for a function unrelated to its business.
 No business nexus under Section 16(1).
 23. Exempt outward activity
 Catering directly attributable to exempt supplies.
 Section 17(2) restricts related credit.
 24. Taxable + exempt activities
 Common catering cost supports both taxable and exempt operations.
 Apportionment may be required under Section 17(2).
 25. Restaurant meals
 Ordinary restaurant lunch during a business meeting.
 Separate food/beverages block not expressly relaxed.
 26. Invalid documentation
 Company lacks a qualifying tax invoice.
 Section 16 and invoice requirements.
 27. Wrong registration
 Tax invoice issued to another GSTIN and claimed in wrong GST registration.
 Registration-specific eligibility rules.
 28. Catering in another State
 Delhi business has event in Haryana catered there.
 Place-of-supply and relevant State/IGST credit position require review.
 29. Time-barred invoice
 Claim attempted after Section 16(4) deadline.
 Statutory time limit unless exception applies.
 30. Supplier charged no GST
 Invoice reflects no tax.
 No corresponding GST input tax to credit.
 31. Mixed business/private
 Corporate event includes substantial personal hospitality.
 Non-business portion may be excluded/apportioned.
 Place of Supply: Cross-State Catering
 For catering services governed by Section 12(4) of the IGST Act, the place of supply is generally where the services are actually performed.
 For example, where catering is physically performed at a conference in Haryana, the place of supply will ordinarily be Haryana.
 However, the place of supply alone does not determine whether Haryana CGST/SGST or IGST must be charged. 
 The tax type will also depend upon the location of the supplier.
 Where the caterer is located in Haryana and the service is performed in Haryana, the transaction may attract Haryana CGST and SGST.
 Where the caterer is located in Delhi but the catering service is performed in Haryana, the supplier location and place of supply are in different States and the transaction would ordinarily be treated as inter-State, attracting IGST.
 The recipient must therefore examine the precise supplier and recipient locations, invoice GSTIN, place of supply, nature of tax charged and the GST registration in which credit is sought.
 The proposed blocked-credit amendment would not change the place-of-supply rules.

 In this illustration, the annual amount of GST affected is up to Rs. 2,00,000.
 Actual eligibility will depend on the classification of each supply, legally effective amendment, business/exempt usage and compliance with other statutory conditions.
 8. Documents to Retain for Different Cases
 Scenario 
 Supporting records 
 Dealers' conference
 Invitations, event agenda, attendance details, contract and invoice
 Product launch
 Marketing approval, programme details, event records and invoice
 Employee training
 Training agenda, employee attendance, catering contract and invoice
 Corporate meetings
 Meeting agenda, approval, participants and supplier invoice
 Mandatory factory canteen
 Applicable legal obligation, employee strength, contract, invoices and records
 Employee-subsidised canteen
 Employer-cost share, employee recoveries, contractual policy and ITC working
 Outward taxable catering
 Customer contract, supplier invoice and outward taxable invoices
 Composite/mixed outward supply
 Customer scope of work, package description and taxable invoices
 Interstate catering
 Supplier/recipient locations, correct GSTIN, place-of-supply position
 General eligibility conditions under Section 16 also apply, including the tax invoice, receipt of service, relevant invoice communication/reporting, tax and return requirements, payment conditions and applicable ITC time limit.
 9. Earlier Years, Commencement and Transitional Credits
 The GST Council recommendation does not expressly grant retrospective relief or prescribe the commencement date for the outdoor-catering change.
 Businesses cannot now reclaim ITC previously blocked for FY 2023 - 24, FY 2024 - 25 or FY 2025 - 26 merely on the basis of the press release.
 Prior-year recovery, if any, will depend on the enacted text, commencement, possible transitional/retrospective clauses and Section 16(4) time limits.
 10. One-page Summary of Key Scenarios
 Situation 
 Existing law 
 After proposed change 
 Statutorily obligatory factory canteen
 May already be eligible
 Existing exception may continue
 Voluntary office canteen
 Generally blocked
 Eligibility depends on final wording and whether supply qualifies as outdoor catering rather than separately restricted food/beverages or other contract food service
 Dealer meetings, sales events
 Generally blocked
 Potentially eligible
 Employee training / product launch
 Generally blocked
 Potentially eligible
 Further outward taxable catering
 Statutory exception; rate conditions apply
 Rate conditions still relevant
 Catering in taxable composite/mixed supply
 Exception may apply
 Other requirements continue
 Director's private celebration
 Disallowed
 Disallowed
 Services attributable to exempt supplies
 Restricted
 Restricted
 Ordinary restaurant meals
 Generally restricted
 No express general relaxation
 Invalid/late invoice
 Disallowed or restricted
 Still subject to Section 16
 11. Conclusion
 The proposed Section 17(5)(b)(i) relaxation could materially reduce non-creditable GST on business-related outdoor catering.
 Its greatest potential benefit is for ordinary companies arranging conferences, dealer meetings, sales events, training programmes and other genuine business events that do not satisfy the existing exceptions.
 However, the proposal is not a blanket ITC entitlement on food, meals, canteen services or hospitality. 
 In particular, the classification of an employee-canteen or continuing food-service arrangement should be examined before assuming that it falls within the proposed outdoor-catering relaxation. The separate food-and-beverages restriction, personal-consumption bar, business-use requirement, rules for exempt supplies, Section 16 conditions, service-rate restrictions and place-of-supply rules must each be evaluated.
 Existing exceptions for genuine outward taxable supplies and legally required employee canteens should also not be overlooked.
 As at 14 October 2026, the Council recommendation has not become operative law and no specific effective date has been announced for this change.
 The final enacted wording will govern eligibility and any possible benefit for earlier periods.
